sections.body:
Culture shock is the disorientation you feel when the everyday rules of a place stop being the rules you grew up with. It is not homesickness in the ordinary sense. Homesickness means you miss what you know. Culture shock means you can no longer predict what is about to happen, and that turns small interactions into effort.

The surprise rarely comes from the big things. Nobody expects a different language or a different currency. What surprises people is the ordinary machinery of daily life: whether to shake hands, how late a shop stays open, whether a stranger says hello on the street, how loud a restaurant is at eight in the evening, whether you are expected to remove your shoes at the door of a private home.

Researchers usually describe four stages. The **honeymoon** stage comes first: everything is interesting, new and slightly exciting. The **frustration** stage follows, when the novelty wears off and the small differences become tiring. Then comes **adjustment**, when you start learning the practical rules and stop being surprised by most days. The last stage is **adaptation**, when the place feels ordinary and you have your own routines there.

Most people who suffer badly are not the ones who dislike the country. They are the ones who expect their own habits to be the default everywhere and read every difference as a mistake. The habit that protects you is simple: treat the local way as the way things are done here, and your way as the way things are done at home. Neither is better. They are just different sets of instructions.
examples: In this country people greet each other in the street, so I greet them too.
It felt strange for a week, and then it felt normal.
sections.heading: What culture shock actually is

sections.body:
Almost every visitor is caught by the same short list. Learn it before you arrive and you will save yourself weeks of small embarrassments.

Greetings. In some countries a handshake, a nod, a kiss on both cheeks and a bow are all normal, and the choice depends on who you are greeting and how well you know them. In others, a greeting is a full stop: you say hello, you say it once, and you do not repeat it every time you meet someone in the same day. Guessing wrong is rarely a disaster, but noticing the pattern is what makes you feel at home.

Meals. The shape of a meal changes more than the food. Some places serve everything at once and expect the group to share. Some serve dish by dish, in order, and the courses set the pace of the evening. Some expect you to eat with a spoon and a fork together. Some require you to wait for the host to start. In Vietnam, for example, a shared bowl of phở is lifted by whoever needs it, while a formal meal in Japan runs in fixed order and the smallest bite comes last.

Queueing. Most countries queue, but the shape of the queue varies. It may be a physical line, or a system of who was here first remembered by the person in front of you. In some places, being served out of order is normal and unremarkable. In others, pushing forward is a serious breach of manners.

Quiet hours. Many countries have a stretch of the day when nothing loud happens: a school recess, a siesta, a period after lunch in the office, a worship call. Shops close, voices drop, and phones go silent. If you walk through that window at full volume you are the outsider, and you will be told so.

Time. Punctuality is where cultures differ most sharply, and where visitors draw the wrong conclusion fastest. Being fifteen minutes late means nothing in one country and is an apology in another. Watch how people treat an appointment before you decide what punctuality means there.
examples: Would you like me to take my shoes off?
Is it all right to call you by your first name?
I am sorry, I did not know we eat in courses.
sections.heading: The everyday things that surprise people first

sections.body:
Time is where most misunderstandings begin, because every culture has an unwritten schedule and no country publishes it.

Compare three working weeks. In much of northern Europe the week is short, the hours are protected, and a meeting that starts at 09:00 is a meeting that starts at 09:00. In the United States the working day is long and the calendar is thin, so people work late and take fewer days off. Across much of Southeast Asia and the Gulf, the working week runs from Sunday to Thursday or Friday, the weekend is short, and the working day is split by a long midday break. In Spain and much of Latin America, the afternoon is a different part of the day from the morning, and nobody expects a decision at 17:00.

The meeting itself has rules too. In some cultures the decision is made in the meeting and the meeting is short. In others the real decision was made before the meeting, and the meeting exists to record it. If you arrive expecting to decide something and everyone else expects to confirm something, you will spend the hour confused.

A second difference is the meaning of a free evening. In some places the evening is family time and the whole street empties. In others the evening is when the work happens, because everyone else is asleep.

The practical method is to ask, once, early. Ask what time a meeting should end, when the office empties, when the shop closes. Ask the question plainly and you will almost always get a clear answer, because these are ordinary questions and everybody has a habit you are trying to learn.
examples: What time should the meeting finish for everyone?
Is the office quiet in the afternoon?
Would it be better to call you earlier in the morning?
sections.heading: Time, punctuality and the working week

sections.body:
These words appear in books and in conversations with people who have moved abroad. Knowing them helps you ask better questions.

Culture shock is the disorientation that comes from the local rules no longer matching your expectations. **Ethnocentrism** is the habit of judging another culture by the standards of your own, and treating any difference as a defect rather than a choice.

Adaptation is the finished state: you have learned the local way well enough to act without thinking about it. **Adjustment** is the work you do while getting there.

Social norm is a rule that everybody follows without discussing it, such as taking shoes off indoors. A **taboo** is a line that is not crossed at all, such as discussing a person's salary. **Etiquette** is the visible part: how you are expected to behave at a table, at a door, at a gift.

Small talk is the neutral conversation people use to make contact, and it is different in every language. **Stereotype** is the shared shortcut people use about a group. **Prejudice** is the negative attitude that comes with it. Both are quicker than real knowledge, which is why they fill the gap while you learn.

FOMO is the fear of missing out, borrowed from social media. **Homesickness** is missing people and places. **Culture fatigue** is the exhaustion that comes from living in a language and a set of rules that are not yours, and it is a real condition rather than a complaint.
examples: It is not culture shock, it is just a different custom.
I did not know that was a taboo, so I stopped asking about it.
sections.heading: The words people use for the experience

terms.example: Culture shock hit me the week I could not find a supermarket open after six.
terms.gloss: The disorientation you feel when the everyday rules of a place stop matching the ones you grew up with.

terms.example: Calling a local custom rude is ethnocentrism, not an observation.
terms.gloss: Judging another culture by the standards of your own, and reading every difference as a mistake.

terms.example: The norm here is to arrive ten minutes late, and everyone reads the time differently.
terms.gloss: A rule everybody follows without discussing it, such as removing shoes before entering a home.

terms.example: Asking about his pay was a taboo, so I did not ask.
terms.gloss: A line that is not crossed at all, such as asking about somebody's salary.

terms.example: A comment about the weather is small talk, and in some countries it is the only small talk you get.
terms.gloss: Neutral conversation used to make contact. The rules for it differ in every language.

terms.example: After a year, adaptation: I queue without thinking about it now.
terms.gloss: The finished state of living comfortably in a new culture, when the local way no longer feels strange.

sections.body:
You will meet a practice that annoys you. The procedure is not to swallow it silently, and not to announce that it is ridiculous. There is a middle way, and it is the same one you would use in your own country with a colleague you disagree with.

First, find out whether it is actually a rule or only one person's habit. Ask two people from different families. If the answers agree, it is the rule.

Second, separate the practice from the people. You are not saying the country is badly run. You are saying a custom caught you out. That sentence keeps the conversation friendly, and it is true.

Third, do it anyway when the cost is low. If the custom is to arrive ten minutes late, arrive ten minutes late. Adapting for a year is cheaper than explaining for a year. Save your objection for the things that actually cost you something.

Fourth, when you need to refuse, refuse the practice and not the person, and give a reason that belongs to you. "I am not comfortable with this" is a complete reason and needs nothing else. "That is wrong" starts a fight you cannot win.

Fifth, watch the reaction of people who live there. They are not defending a national pride; they are defending a habit that saves them effort. When you understand what the habit is for, you often stop disliking it.
examples: I am not comfortable with this, so I will sit apart.
Is this something everybody does, or just your family?
I did not know, thank you. I will do it your way this time.
sections.heading: How to be polite when something feels wrong

sections.body:
Almost nobody plans their arrival well, and almost everybody can do better with a short list. Work through this in order, and you will spend your first weeks learning instead of recovering.

The order matters. Learning the practical rules first saves you from the exhaustion of being surprised by small things all day, and it leaves the emotional energy for the deeper adjustments that come later.
examples: What do visitors usually get wrong in this country?
I am going to copy the way you greet people here.
sections.heading: How to get through your first three weeks
steps: Learn the greetings, the thanks and the basic politeness words before you land.
Find out the working hours, the quiet hours and the weekend in your first week.
Watch three ordinary routines: a meal, a queue and a meeting.
Ask one local person what visitors usually get wrong here.
Write down the differences that keep surprising you, and check each one against reality.
Choose two local habits to copy, and keep everything else in your own file.

sections.body: Do not assume that silence means refusal, that a quiet shop is closed, that a refusal was personal, or that a different custom means a careless or rude person. Most of these readings come from a rule you learned somewhere else, applied to a situation that does not follow it. Do not generalise about a country from one person, one shop or one bad day. Do not let a loud traveller set the standard for everybody. And do not wait until you are angry to ask: the moment you notice the confusion is the cheapest moment to resolve it.
sections.heading: What not to assume in your first weeks

sections.body:
Here is the part most advice leaves out. When something surprises you abroad, the surprise is often about you, not about them. A custom rarely surprises only one visitor. It surprises every person whose home rules are different, and it stops surprising the people who live there, which is why the custom exists at all.

So when a local says that a practice is normal, they are not being defensive. They are describing a system that they grew up inside, exactly as you grew up inside yours. The person who finds a Vietnamese family meal astonishing is not making a clever observation; they are comparing two rulebooks they happen to hold in different hands.

This has a practical consequence. The more precisely you can describe your own habit, the better you can read theirs. "In my country we take our shoes off in the hallway, so I was surprised that yours stay on" is a good sentence. "Your country is so strange" is not, because it ends the conversation.

The other half of the point is that the surprise can be about power. A visitor usually has money, mobility and status that a local does not. When a custom seems strange, ask whether it makes sense for the people who have to live with it. A custom that protects strangers, women or children is doing a job you cannot see from outside.
examples: In my country we always take our shoes off at the door, so I was surprised.
Is that rule to protect the floor, or to protect the guests?
sections.heading: Why the surprise is not really about the country

sections.body:
Many people find that the hardest part of living abroad is not the arrival but the return. You leave a country where you had a routine, a landlord who knew your name, a shop where they held your order, and a language you could argue in. You come back to a place that has changed while you were away, and to a version of yourself that now has different habits.

The symptom is common and has a name: **re-entry shock**. You feel awkward with your own family. The food at home is wrong, and you start cooking the way you cooked abroad. The supermarket is too bright. Your friends have not changed and you have, so the conversation goes in circles.

Three things help. The first is to expect it, because a surprise makes the feeling worse than the fact. The second is to give the difference time. Adjustment on the way out took weeks; on the way back it takes weeks too, and it is shorter than you think. The third is to use what you learned while you were away. Knowing why another culture does something strange is exactly what makes you able to explain your own strange habits to somebody else, and that conversation is a good place to start again.

Do not expect the place to be exactly as you left it. Some of the change is in the country and some of it is in you, and both are real.
examples: It took me a month to stop arranging my kitchen the old way.
My friends had not changed, but I had.
sections.heading: Coming home: the second shock

sections.body:
The point of learning about culture shock is not to become an expert on other countries. It is to be able to walk into a new place and function without wasting your energy on small mistakes.

Take the surprise you hit hardest in your first week. Write it down. Then write down the rule that explains it, in one sentence, in the language of the place. Then find one physical thing you can do differently tomorrow: greet differently, ask for the bill differently, arrive at a different time.

Then make it a habit rather than an exception. Habits are what carry you through weeks two, three and ten, when the novelty is gone and nothing is interesting any more. A rule you have practised ten times is worth more than a rule you understood once.

After that, look for the reverse. There will be a local custom that you adopt so completely that you forget it was foreign, and a visitor from your country will be surprised by it. That moment, when you become the odd one for somebody else, is the clearest sign that you have adapted.

And keep one habit of asking. The people you meet are not a data source to be mined; they are the people who will teach you the rules you cannot read. Asking one good question costs nothing and saves a week.
examples: From now on I will greet people the way people here do.
The best thing I learned abroad was how to ask without feeling awkward.
Now I am the one who explains the rule to visitors.
sections.heading: Turning one surprise into a working habit

item.summary: Moving to a new country changes small things before big ones: greetings, meals, punctuality, silence. After reading this you can name what is surprising you, tell a personal habit from a local rule, and handle the first weeks without assuming that your way is the correct one.
item.title: Culture Shock: Things That Surprise People Abroad
